---
title: "A5 exercises — Nerve, muscle, hormones and reproduction"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Membrane potential

### 1.1

The Nernst equation at 37 °C is

$$E_\text{ion} = \frac{61.5\ \text{mV}}{z}\,\log_{10}\frac{[\text{ion}]_\text{out}}{[\text{ion}]_\text{in}},$$

where $z$ is the charge of the ion. Calculate the equilibrium potential of
each ion in a mammalian neuron.

| Ion | Outside (mmol L⁻¹) | Inside (mmol L⁻¹) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| K⁺ | 5 | 140 |
| Na⁺ | 145 | 15 |
| Cl⁻ | 110 | 10 |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- $E_\text{K} = 61.5 \log_{10}(5/140) = 61.5 \times (-1.45) \approx -89$ mV.
- $E_\text{Na} = 61.5 \log_{10}(145/15) = 61.5 \times 0.985 \approx +61$ mV.
- $E_\text{Cl} = -61.5 \log_{10}(110/10) = -61.5 \times 1.04 \approx -64$ mV
  ($z = -1$).
:::

### 1.2

The neuron in 1.1 has a resting membrane potential of −70 mV.

a. Which ion's equilibrium potential is the resting potential closest to, and
   what does this tell you about the resting membrane?
b. In which direction is the net electrochemical driving force on Na⁺?
c. In which direction is the net electrochemical driving force on K⁺?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. K⁺. At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ (through leak
   channels) than to Na⁺.
b. Inward: both the concentration gradient and the negative inside favour Na⁺
   entry.
c. Outward. The membrane potential (−70 mV) is less negative than $E_\text{K}$
   (−89 mV), so the concentration gradient outweighs the electrical attraction.
:::

### 1.3

Extracellular K⁺ is raised from 5 to 10 mmol L⁻¹ (intracellular K⁺ stays at
140 mmol L⁻¹). Calculate the new $E_\text{K}$. Does the membrane depolarise or
hyperpolarise?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$E_\text{K} = 61.5 \log_{10}(10/140) \approx -70.5$ mV. $E_\text{K}$ becomes
less negative, so the resting membrane depolarises.
:::

### 1.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP.
b. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase directly produces the rising phase of the action
   potential.
c. The inside of a resting neuron is negative because all the molecules in
   the cytoplasm are negatively charged.
d. During a single action potential, the intracellular Na⁺ concentration
   changes only very slightly.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. True.
b. False. The rising phase is caused by Na⁺ flowing in through voltage-gated
   Na⁺ channels, down its electrochemical gradient. The pump maintains the
   gradients over the longer term.
c. False. The cytoplasm as a whole is electrically neutral; only a very small
   excess of negative charge lies next to the membrane.
d. True. Very few ions need to cross the membrane to change the voltage.
:::

## The action potential

### 2.1

Put the events of an axonal action potential in order.

a. Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell.
b. The membrane is depolarised to threshold.
c. The membrane briefly hyperpolarises below the resting potential.
d. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ enters the cell.
e. Na⁺ channels inactivate.
f. The membrane potential rises rapidly and becomes positive (overshoot).
g. K⁺ channels close and the resting potential is restored.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → f → e → a → c → g. Na⁺-channel inactivation and K⁺-channel opening
together cause repolarisation.
:::

### 2.2

Define the *absolute* and the *relative refractory period*, and give the cause
of each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Absolute refractory period:** no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a
  second action potential. Cause: the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are
  inactivated.
- **Relative refractory period:** a stronger-than-normal stimulus is needed
  to trigger an action potential. Cause: some Na⁺ channels are still
  inactivated and K⁺ conductance is still raised (the membrane is
  hyperpolarised).

The refractory period makes the action potential travel in one direction
only.
:::

### 2.3

A stronger stimulus is applied to a sensory receptor. Which two properties of
the sensory signal increase? Which property stays the same?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The frequency of action potentials in each neuron and the number of neurons
recruited both increase. The amplitude of each action potential stays the
same, because the action potential is all-or-none.
:::

### 2.4

a. Name two properties of an axon that increase its conduction velocity.
b. An action potential travels 0.60 m from the spinal cord to a foot muscle
   in 12 ms. Calculate the conduction velocity in m s⁻¹.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. A larger axon diameter, and myelination (saltatory conduction between nodes
   of Ranvier).
b. 0.60 m ÷ 0.012 s = 50 m s⁻¹.
:::

## Synapses and reflexes

### 3.1

Put the events at a chemical synapse in order.

a. Transmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
b. Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open in the presynaptic terminal.
c. An action potential arrives at the presynaptic terminal.
d. Synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release
   transmitter by exocytosis.
e. Ca²⁺ enters the terminal.
f. Ion channels open and the postsynaptic membrane potential changes.
g. Transmitter is removed by enzymatic breakdown or reuptake.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

c → b → e → d → a → f → g.
:::

### 3.2

State whether each postsynaptic response is excitatory or inhibitory.

a. Acetylcholine opens cation channels (nicotinic receptors) on a skeletal
   muscle fibre.
b. Acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptors on cardiac pacemaker cells and
   opens K⁺ channels.
c. GABA opens Cl⁻ channels, and the membrane potential moves towards
   $E_\text{Cl}$ (−70 mV) from a threshold of −55 mV.
d. Glutamate opens channels permeable to Na⁺ and K⁺.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Excitatory. b. Inhibitory (it slows the heart). c. Inhibitory.
d. Excitatory.

Examples a and b show that the same transmitter can excite or inhibit: the
effect depends on the receptor.
:::

### 3.3

Name each component of the knee-jerk (patellar) reflex.

| Component | Structure in the knee-jerk reflex |
| --- | --- |
| Receptor | |
| Afferent pathway | |
| Integrating centre | |
| Efferent pathway | |
| Effector | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Component | Structure in the knee-jerk reflex |
| --- | --- |
| Receptor | Muscle spindle (stretch receptor) in the quadriceps |
| Afferent pathway | Sensory neuron |
| Integrating centre | Spinal cord (one synapse: a monosynaptic reflex) |
| Efferent pathway | Motor neuron |
| Effector | Quadriceps muscle |

The reflex does not need the brain, so it is faster than a voluntary
response.
:::

## Skeletal muscle

### 4.1

Put the steps of excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle in order.

a. Ca²⁺ binds to troponin.
b. Acetylcholine is released at the neuromuscular junction.
c. Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
d. An action potential arrives at the motor-neuron terminal.
e. Tropomyosin moves and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin.
f. The muscle action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and into the
   T tubules.
g. Myosin heads bind actin and perform power strokes.
h. An end-plate potential depolarises the muscle fibre to threshold.
i. Voltage-sensing (dihydropyridine) receptors in the T-tubule membrane open
   the ryanodine receptors of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

d → b → h → f → i → c → a → e → g.

Relaxation follows when acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase
and Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by an ATP-driven
Ca²⁺ pump.
:::

### 4.2

Give the role of each step in the cross-bridge cycle.

a. ATP binding to myosin
b. ATP hydrolysis by myosin
c. Release of phosphate from myosin

Why do muscles become rigid after death (rigor mortis)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Detaches the myosin head from actin.
b. Re-cocks the myosin head into its high-energy position.
c. Triggers the power stroke, which pulls the thin filament towards the
   centre of the sarcomere.

After death ATP runs out, so myosin heads stay bound to actin and cannot
detach.
:::

### 4.3

When a sarcomere shortens, which of the following become shorter and which
stay the same length?

a. A band
b. I band
c. H zone
d. Distance between Z discs
e. Thick (myosin) filaments
f. Thin (actin) filaments

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Shorter: b, c and d. Unchanged: a, e and f. The filaments slide past each
other without changing length (sliding-filament model).
:::

### 4.4

A muscle lifts a load with a constant force of 20 N through 0.10 m in
0.50 s, with force and displacement in the same direction. It then holds the
load still for 5 s.

a. Calculate the external mechanical work done while lifting.
b. Calculate the mean external mechanical power while lifting.
c. Calculate the external work done while holding the load still.
d. True or false: the muscle uses no ATP while holding the load still.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. $W = Fd = 20 \times 0.10 = 2.0$ J.
b. $P = W/t = 2.0 / 0.50 = 4.0$ W.
c. 0 J, because there is no displacement.
d. False. Cross-bridges keep cycling to maintain force (isometric
   contraction), and Ca²⁺ pumping continues, so ATP is consumed.
:::

### 4.5

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. A motor unit is one motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it
   innervates.
b. Whole-muscle force can be increased by recruiting more motor units.
c. Whole-muscle force can be increased by raising the frequency of action
   potentials, so that twitches summate into tetanus.
d. Whole-muscle force is increased by making each motor-neuron action
   potential larger.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. True. b. True. c. True.
d. False. Action potentials are all-or-none; force is graded by recruitment
   and firing frequency.
:::

### 4.6

In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺ also triggers contraction, but not through troponin.
Name the Ca²⁺-binding protein and the enzyme it activates, and state what
the enzyme does.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin. Ca²⁺–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase
(MLCK), which phosphorylates the myosin light chains. This allows myosin to
bind actin and cycle.
:::

## Nervous systems and hormones

### 5.1

Match each animal with its type of nervous system.

| | Animal |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | *Hydra* (cnidarian) |
| 2 | Earthworm |
| 3 | Mammal |

| | Nervous system |
| --- | --- |
| A | Brain and spinal cord (dorsal, hollow nerve cord) forming a CNS, plus a peripheral nervous system |
| B | Diffuse nerve net with no brain |
| C | Cerebral ganglia and a ventral nerve cord with a ganglion in each segment |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1–B, 2–C, 3–A.
:::

### 5.2

Complete the table comparing two classes of hormone.

| | Peptide hormones | Steroid hormones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solubility | | |
| Transport in blood | | |
| Location of receptor | | |
| Main mechanism of action | | |
| Two examples | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Peptide hormones | Steroid hormones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solubility | Water-soluble | Lipid-soluble |
| Transport in blood | Dissolved in plasma | Mostly bound to carrier proteins |
| Location of receptor | Cell surface (plasma membrane) | Inside the cell (cytoplasm or nucleus) |
| Main mechanism of action | Second messengers (e.g. cAMP) alter the activity of existing proteins | Hormone–receptor complex binds DNA and changes gene transcription |
| Two examples | Insulin, ADH (also LH, FSH, oxytocin) | Cortisol, testosterone (also oestradiol, progesterone, aldosterone) |

A cell responds to a hormone only if it has the matching receptor, so the
same hormone concentration can affect one tissue and not another.
:::

### 5.3

Name the gland (or cells) that secretes each hormone.

a. GnRH
b. LH and FSH
c. ADH and oxytocin (site of release into the blood)
d. Testosterone
e. Progesterone after ovulation
f. Insulin
g. Adrenaline
h. Cortisol

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Hypothalamus.
b. Anterior pituitary.
c. Posterior pituitary (the hormones are made by hypothalamic neurons).
d. Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testis.
e. Corpus luteum of the ovary.
f. β cells of the pancreatic islets.
g. Adrenal medulla.
h. Adrenal cortex.
:::

## Reproduction

### 6.1

Complete the table for the mammalian hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis.

| Hormone | Target cells | Main effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GnRH | | |
| LH in the male | | |
| FSH in the male | | |
| FSH in the female | | |
| LH surge in the female | | |
| Inhibin | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Hormone | Target cells | Main effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GnRH | Gonadotroph cells of the anterior pituitary | Stimulates LH and FSH secretion |
| LH in the male | Leydig cells | Stimulates testosterone secretion |
| FSH in the male | Sertoli cells | Supports spermatogenesis |
| FSH in the female | Granulosa cells of the follicle | Stimulates follicle growth and oestradiol production |
| LH surge in the female | Mature (Graafian) follicle | Triggers ovulation and formation of the corpus luteum |
| Inhibin | Anterior pituitary | Inhibits FSH secretion |
:::

### 6.2

State whether each example is negative or positive feedback.

a. Testosterone inhibits GnRH and LH secretion.
b. A sustained high oestradiol concentration late in the follicular phase
   triggers the LH surge.
c. Progesterone from the corpus luteum inhibits GnRH, LH and FSH secretion.
d. Inhibin reduces FSH secretion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Negative. b. Positive. c. Negative. d. Negative.
:::

### 6.3

Put the events of the human ovarian cycle in order, starting at the beginning
of the follicular phase.

a. Ovulation
b. Oestradiol concentration rises to a high level
c. The corpus luteum forms and secretes progesterone and oestradiol
d. FSH stimulates the growth of several follicles
e. The LH surge
f. Without pregnancy, the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone falls
g. Menstruation begins and FSH rises again

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

d → b → e → a → c → f → g.
:::

## Explore: Ion gradients and membrane potential {#explore-a5-membrane}

The left panel shows K⁺ (green) and Na⁺ (red) on both sides of the membrane,
with the channel widths showing the relative permeability; the right panel
places $E_\text{K}$, $E_\text{Na}$ (Nernst) and the membrane potential $V_m$
(Goldman equation) on one voltage scale. Use the sliders or the preset buttons,
and read the values from the readout below the buttons.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a5-membrane" data-preset="rest"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a5-membrane.js"></script>
```

### E1.1

Click **Rest**. Read off $E_\text{K}$, $E_\text{Na}$ and $V_m$. Is $V_m$ closer
to $E_\text{K}$ or to $E_\text{Na}$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$E_\text{K}$ = −89 mV, $E_\text{Na}$ = +61 mV, $V_m$ = −69 mV (the same values
as in 1.1). $V_m$ is much closer to $E_\text{K}$, because at rest
$P_\text{Na}/P_\text{K}$ is only 0.04.
:::

### E1.2

Click **K⁺ channels only** ($P_\text{Na}/P_\text{K} \approx 0$). What is $V_m$
now, and what is the K⁺ driving force?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$V_m$ = −88 mV, practically equal to $E_\text{K}$ (−89 mV); the K⁺ driving
force is only +1 mV. A membrane permeable to one ion only sits at that ion's
Nernst potential.
:::

### E1.3

Click **Rest**, then drag **K⁺ outside** from 5 to 10. Read off $E_\text{K}$ and
$V_m$. Then click **K⁺ out = 20** and read them again. Does raising
extracellular K⁺ depolarise or hyperpolarise the cell?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| K⁺ outside (mmol L⁻¹) | $E_\text{K}$ | $V_m$ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | −89 mV | −69 mV |
| 10 | −70 mV | −58 mV |
| 20 | −52 mV | −45 mV |

It depolarises the cell (compare 1.3). This is why hyperkalaemia is dangerous:
excitable cells, including heart muscle, are pushed towards and past threshold.
:::

### E1.4

Click **Na⁺ channels open** ($P_\text{Na}/P_\text{K}$ = 20). What is $V_m$? Did
the number of ion dots on either side change noticeably?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

$V_m$ = +50 mV, close to $E_\text{Na}$ (+61 mV), as at the peak of an action
potential. The dots do not change: the potential reverses through a change in
permeability, not in concentration; very few ions need to cross.
:::

### E1.5

Click **Rest**, then set $P_\text{Na}/P_\text{K}$ to 1 (equal permeabilities).
Which value is closest to $V_m$: −89, −69, −1 or +61 mV?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

−1 mV. With equal permeabilities $V_m$ lies roughly midway between
$E_\text{K}$ and $E_\text{Na}$: the membrane potential is a
permeability-weighted compromise between the equilibrium potentials.
:::

## Explore: Threshold and refractory periods {#explore-a5-spike}

A Hodgkin–Huxley axon receives two brief current pulses, S1 and S2 (each
0.5 ms). Set their strengths and the S1 → S2 interval with the sliders or the
preset buttons. The lower panel shows the fraction of Na⁺ channels that are not
inactivated (green) and the open K⁺ channels (gold); the verdict and readout
below the buttons report the spikes.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a5-spike" data-a1="40" data-a2="40" data-gap="3"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a5-spike.js"></script>
```

### E2.1

Click **Too weak** (S1 = 12, no S2), then raise **S1 strength** one step at a
time. What is the smallest S1 that produces a spike?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

16. At 15 the membrane depolarises a little and returns to rest; at 16 a full
spike follows. This is the threshold.
:::

### E2.2

Click **One spike** (S1 = 40) and read the peak Vm. Then set S1 to 20 and to 80.
What happens to the peak?

a. It roughly doubles from S1 = 20 to S1 = 80.
b. It stays about the same (+26 to +32 mV).
c. The spike disappears at S1 = 80.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Peak Vm is +30 mV at S1 = 40, +26 mV at 20 and +32 mV at 80. Above
threshold the spike is all-or-none: a stronger stimulus does not give a bigger
spike (stimulus strength is coded by spike frequency instead). The lowest Vm,
the undershoot, is −81 mV in every case.
:::

### E2.3

Click **2nd at 1.5 ms, 8×** (S2 = 320, eight times S1). Is there a second spike?
Which refractory period is this, and what does the green trace show?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No second spike, even at S2 = 320: the absolute refractory period. The green
trace shows that almost all Na⁺ channels are still inactivated, so no stimulus
can open enough of them.
:::

### E2.4

Click **2nd at 3 ms** (S2 = 40). Does S2 fire? According to the verdict, what
S2 strength is needed at this interval? Then click **3 ms, 2× stronger**: how
many spikes now?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

S2 = 40 fails; the verdict says S2 needs about 60 (relative refractory period).
At S2 = 80 there are 2 spikes. In the relative refractory period a spike is
possible, but only with a stronger stimulus, because some Na⁺ channels are
still inactivated and K⁺ channels are still open.
:::

### E2.5

Keep S1 = S2 = 40 and drag **S1 → S2** upwards from 2 ms in 0.5 ms steps. At
which interval does the second spike first appear?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

At 4.0 ms (at 3.5 ms S2 would need about 45). Refractoriness limits the maximum
spike frequency and makes spikes travel in one direction only.
:::

## Explore: Summation, tetanus and recruitment {#explore-a5-twitch}

The plot shows the force of a muscle of four motor units (sizes 1 to 4, stacked
colours) when its motor neurons fire at the chosen rate for 500 ms; red ticks
below are the spikes. Set **Stimulus rate** (0 = one stimulus) and **Motor
units** with the sliders or buttons and read the verdict and readout.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="a5-twitch" data-hz="0" data-units="4"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/a5-twitch.js"></script>
```

### E3.1

With 4 motor units, click **5 Hz**, **15 Hz**, **30 Hz** and **80 Hz** in turn.
For each, give the verdict and the "peak force / one twitch" value.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Rate | Verdict | Peak force / one twitch |
| ---: | --- | ---: |
| 5 Hz | Separate twitches | 1.0× |
| 15 Hz | Summation: unfused tetanus | 1.6× |
| 30 Hz | Fused tetanus | 2.4× |
| 80 Hz | Fused tetanus | 3.4× |

At higher rates Ca²⁺ is released again before the previous release has been
pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so the twitches summate.
:::

### E3.2

Drag the rate slider upwards from 20 Hz. At which rate does the verdict first
change to "Fused tetanus"?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

30 Hz. Force keeps rising beyond that (2.4× at 30 Hz, 3.4× at 80 Hz) even
though the trace is already smooth.
:::

### E3.3

Set the rate to 80 Hz. Read the peak total force with 1, 2, 3 and 4 motor units
recruited. Which unit adds the largest step?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

0.9, 2.8, 5.7 and 9.4. The fourth (largest) unit adds the largest step (3.7).
Units are recruited smallest first (size principle), so force is graded finely
at low force and in large steps at high force.
:::

### E3.4

Click **Single twitch** with 4 units, then **80 Hz** with 4 units. Which of the
following changed between the two runs?

a. The size of each motor-neuron spike
b. The number of motor-neuron spikes
c. The number of motor units recruited

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Only b (1 stimulus versus 40). Peak total force rose from 2.8 to 9.4 because
the muscle summates many twitches; spikes are all-or-none and never got bigger.
Muscle force is graded by firing rate and by recruitment (c, not changed here).
:::
